chapter_theme: First songs at Vayalur (வயலூர், வயலி, 1 of 2), the shrine near Trichy on the Kaveri where the poet places his own call: courtesans who show, sell and swear, the catalogue of a woman's charms, and the body and kin renounced with 'enough, enough'; against them the poet asks for the teaching of pati, pasu and pasam, for jnana beyond sects and rites, and recalls the Lord who called him at Viralimalai and ruled him in a dream.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (901, 902, 903, 914) and songs of women's charms (905, 906, 909, 910, 913); doctrine (900 on pati-pasu-pasam, 907 against sects and the lower paths, 908 renouncing body and kin); and two songs of the poet's own story (911, 912), with a third (904) that asks 'who am I' in all he does. Two songs (901, 914) and 913's Sambandar praise recur in the next chapters.

900.reading: The poet sets out a litany of homage (நமோ), to Hari's nephew, the one without end, the six-faced Vel, Hara's son, the life of the gods, and says his desire is for the feet; he calls himself a poor man who knows nothing and asks to receive Murugan's teaching of pati, pasu and pasam. The praise shows Chamundi drunk and roaring like the sea as she dances, the rider of elephant and horse hailing Murugan 'victory, victory, commander', and dogs, ghouls, vultures, jackals and crows feasting on the field where Sura fell, at Vayalur by the Kaveri.
900.nuance: பதி பசு பாச உபதேசம் is the Saiva Siddhanta triad named outright as the content of the teaching asked for. ஆடம்பர நாளும் பகர்தல் இலாது may contrast showy daily recitation with the poor man's plea, but the division of that run of syllables is uncertain. The rider of elephant and horse who hails the commander is probably Indra.

901.reading: With the refrain காட்டி ('showing'), the poet lists what women show: breasts, Kama's state, clothes and jewels, alluring eyes, sweet voice, feigned affection to anyone, wet smiles and their arts, until they show the net of their snare; he asks whether that showing of ruin is not enough. The praise plays on வேலை (vel, sea, sport): Murugan fed fire to the forest of Sura's armies, rides the peacock, sent the vel into the sea, wed the virtuous hunter girl of the hill country, and freed the gods, at Vayalur.
901.nuance: The song is built on one verb: the women 'show' everything, and the plea turns the verb on the poet's own ruin (ஈடழிதல் காட்டல் அமையாதோ), which may mean 'is it not enough to have shown me my ruin?' or 'will this showing of ruin not stop?'. சேர மலை நாட்டில் may place Valli in the Chera hill country or simply mean the hill land where they gather.

902.reading: In a long, dense rhythm the poet describes lovemaking in detail, nails, kisses, loosened hair and bird-cries on the bed, and the women who cast the net of their eyes to seize wealth; he asks when Murugan will cut away the grief of Kama's arts and protect him, held in boundless Siva-knowledge, so that he praises in Thiruppugazh. After a battle in drum syllables, the praise names the Kumara of Vayali, Hari's nephew, the six-faced one, and the lord who could tell without error the path of release to the father who dances on the northern peak.
902.nuance: பொருட் கவர கட்டுப் பொறிச்சியர்கள், 'trappers who bind to seize wealth', marks the women as courtesans. The remedy is the book itself: திருப்புகழை உற்றுத் துதிக்கும் வகை. வடகுவடில் நடனமிடும் அப்பர்க்கு முத்திநெறி தப்பற்று உரைக்க is Murugan as Siva's teacher, here of the path to mukti rather than of Om.

903.reading: The poet heaps up epithets for courtesans in rhyming -igal endings: they price their breasts, know many arts, bite lips, join fools for their money, carry eyes like swords that even Yama would find excessive, torment the world, speak of kinship and deceive, and he asks whether they are fit for kinship. The praise is a battlefield of ghouls and demons where Uma bows and the goddess of victory dances, and names Murugan the guru who threw the vel in a moment, lord of the way of knowledge, at Vayali near Trisirapuram.
903.nuance: மடையர் பொருள் பெற மருவிகள், those who join fools to get their money, and உறவு சொலவல துரகிகள் விரகிகள், skilled at talk of kinship and deceit, are the stock charges. The rhyme-chain (அசடிகள் கசடிகள் ... கபடிகள் முகடிகள்) is itself the rhetoric: abuse by sound. த்ரிசிரி கிரி is Trichy's rock, which places Vayali.

904.reading: The poet asks whether it is by him that he is born and dies, praises, calls, walks, sits, enjoys women's houses, tires, burns the disease of attachment, thinks and bears, and ends: who am I here? The praise names Murugan the king who drew fibre from stone, the lord who gave him the word that is nectar to the ear, the vel seen as in a mirror, not dwelling in the minds of the unlearned, son of the gracious Siva who destroyed Daksha, king of the hunter girl and of Vayal town, the one lord over the three.
904.nuance: The repeated என்னால் ('by me') ends in இங்கு நான் ஆர், 'who am I here?': agency is taken from the self, and even the visits to women are listed among acts not the poet's own. கல் நார் உரித்த, drawing fibre from stone, is the softening of a stony heart. கர்ணாமிர்தப் பதம் தந்த கோவே points to the word given the poet at Vayalur. Whether the question is surrender or bewilderment is not said.

905.reading: The poet compares a woman's parts, eyes to the sea and arrows, brow to bow and crescent, lips to fruit and coral, breasts to elephant and hill, waist to creeper and drum, hip to a serpent's hood, and says that by her body, dress and proud walk he whirls in a sorrow where even one day apart is hard; he asks whether he will not escape it. The praise has crows, jackals and ghouls feeding on the demons whose guts were torn out, the gods resettled, and Murugan who loves the daughter of the fierce hill hunters, at Vayalur among fragrant screwpine groves.
905.nuance: The plea names a lover's grief rather than a courtesan's fraud: ஒருநாள் பிரிவது அரிதாய்ச் சுழல்படும் ஒழியாத் துயர், the unending sorrow of one who cannot bear a day's parting. எழில் பாத்திரம் இவள், 'she is a vessel of beauty', gives the woman one direct line.

906.reading: The poet describes golden women like Lakshmi in the lotus, whose camphor-scented breasts, lightning waists, moon faces, dark hair circled by humming bees, bangled shoulders and mango-slice eyes bewilder young men versed in the whole of Kama's quarrelsome lore, and asks whether he must suffer again through them. The praise names the vel that shattered demons, chariots and elephants, the hero praised by ghouls in the forest, the lord of Indra's daughter and the hunter girl, at the beautiful temple of Vayali where the Ganapati of unfailing grace and the holy Lord also dwell.
906.nuance: கலகக் காம நூலை முழுதுணர் இளைஞோர்: the young men are learned in the manual of love, so learning itself is part of the trap. அருளில் சீர் பொய்யாத கணபதி and திருவக்கீசன் point to the shrine's own deities: Vayalur has a Ganapati called Poyyā Ganapati and a Siva called Agnisvara, which is my identification from the names.

907.reading: The poet asks not to perish among impatient men of endless argument, among those who deal in mantra-magic, in the ritual works and rules of conduct that sectarians take up, or even in the chariyai, kiriyai and yoga practised by those devoted to the embodied Lord, but to be given jnana that does not waver. The praise names Murugan as the vel that ended the Diti-born demons' torment of the world, the precious lord of Siva of Thiruvotriyur with the red flame and blue throat, and the supreme beyond maya, bindu, nada and shakti, the god of Mélai Vayali.
907.nuance: The list descends from quarrelling logicians to sectarians and then to the Saiva paths themselves: சரியை க்ரியா யோக நியமத்தின் மாயாது. The first three paths, usually steps toward jnana, become places one can be lost in. சலனப்படா ஞானம், knowledge that does not waver, is set against all of them. மாயை விந்து நாதம் வரசத்தி மேலான பரவத்து puts Murugan above the tattvas of the Siddhanta scheme.

908.reading: With the refrain அலமல ('enough, enough'), the poet renounces the body of blood, worms, water, filth, hair and flesh, its ornaments, perfumes, six-flavoured food and bed, wife, children, mother and kin, all worldly learning but the Siva-lore of the four Vedas, and every tie but with those who think of the Lord; he asks for the knowledge that reaches the shore of the sea of grace. The praise has drums, ghouls and gods crying 'Hara, Siva', names Murugan the nephew of the child who crawled with the mortar and broke the marutha trees, and places him at Viralimalai with its tiger caves and at Vayali where carp leap in the paddy.
908.nuance: The renunciation is ordered from the body outward to food and bed, kin and learning, and keeps only one tie, உனை நினைபவர் உறவு, kinship with those who think of the Lord. The infant Krishna dragging the mortar between the marutha trees (மருது முறிபட உருளும் உரலொடு தவழ்) is told in its unmistakable details.

909.reading: The poet gives the questions of courtship, 'is that a cuckoo's voice, a spear for eyes, a creeper waist?', and the lovemaking with women in their sea of pleasure whom he befriends instead of thinking them enemies, and asks whether, by the grace of Murugan who equals the Pati above pasu and pasam, he will not know the truth. The praise is obscure: it seems to recall Karna, king of Anga and son of the sun, facing the one in a eunuch's guise, and names Murugan the son of Hara and the peacock at Vayalur where the Kaveri carries akil and sandal, lord of the gods of Amaravati.
909.nuance: பகையே என நினையாது உற நண்பு கூரும்: the error is taking enemies for friends. The plea asks for மெய் உணர்தல, knowing the real, through the Pati of the Siddhanta triad. இரவிசேய் எனும் அங்கராசன் is Karna; மயல் பேடிகை may be Arjuna disguised as Brihannala, but how the lines join is not clear to me.

910.reading: The poet speaks of women's kovai-fruit lips, breasts, garland-bearing shoulders, combed and scented hair and carp-like eyes that wither a crore of lives, and asks that, deluded, he not wear himself out daily but be given today the dancing feet that even the faultless Veda cannot find. The praise names Siva, dancer on the bull, consort of the peacock-like Uma, whose feet Vishnu could not find, of fire's colour, as Murugan's father, says Murugan loves Thiruchengodu and Vayali among the lilies, and calls him the one who stops Death's play.
910.nuance: The feet asked for are ஆடல் தாள்கள், dancing feet, and the Veda cannot reach them (ஆசிலாத மறைக்கும் தேடொணாது), as Vishnu could not find Siva's feet in the praise: the plea and the praise share one motif.

911.reading: The poet recalls how Murugan, intending him for his lotus-like feet, came to him on the great hill of Viralimalai crowded with konrai and magizh trees, called 'come', cut away the stain of his mind's desire and gave him the nectar of jnana, and vows never to forget that love. The praise names Murugan the guru of Siva, who burned Kama with his forehead eye, bears the heavenly river in his hair and wears a forest snake as an earring, and the lord of Vayalur, whose vel cut off Sura's head.
911.nuance: This is autobiography, not confession: வா என அழைத்து என் மனது ஆசை மாசினை அறுத்து ஞானமுது அளித்த வாரம் இனி நித்தம் மறவேனே. The call is placed at Viralimalai (அவிராலி மாமலை), though the song is sung at Vayalur, which tradition makes the place of the first call. The pledge is gratitude, not a request.

912.reading: The poet calls himself a sinner of bad conduct, his life pierced by women of beautiful form and deep delusion, and thanks Murugan who ruled him in a dream so that he would not fall into the womb but sing his glory and take up service; he vows never to forget the peacock, the sea of compassion, the faces, the hero's anklets, the kadamba and the vel. The praise names Siva, god of gods, of the name Namasivaya, half woman with the mountain's daughter, as father, Vishnu whose foot measured the fourteen worlds as uncle, and the god of Mélai Vayali in the Chola land ruled by Manu's justice.
912.nuance: கனவில் ஆள் சுவாமீ: the Lord took the poet as his servant in a dream, a second piece of the poet's own story beside 911. கருவிழாது சீரோதி அடிமை பூணலாமாறு gives the purpose: not to fall back into the womb, to sing and to serve. The line on Indra's thunderbolt and elephant is partly corrupt, and whom it names (Devayanai, raised by Indra's elephant?) is not clear.

913.reading: In a run of either-or questions, the poet asks whether a woman's hair is black sand or cloud, her brow a bow or the crescent, her eyes arrows or does, her lips fruit or coral, her breasts pots or hills, her waist a creeper or a drum, her feet flowers or shoots, and confesses wandering vainly in that infatuation; he vows not to forget even once the jewelled-anklet feet. The praise makes Murugan the one who came in the form of the Kaundinya lord of Brahmapuram, learned in Tamil and Veda and praised as Uma's son, when the Buddhists and Jains were ruined, the southern king took the ash and the palm leaf survived the fire, and names him Hari's nephew and Shakti-Ganapati's younger brother, at Vayalur.
913.nuance: The questions (அறலோ முகிலோ, சிலையோ பிறையோ) are the conventional comparisons put as a lover's doubt, so the confession is made from inside the poetry it renounces. பிரமாபுரம் வாழ் கவுணியர் பெருமான் is Sambandar of Sirkazhi of the Kaundinya clan; the ordeal by fire (அனல் ... ஏடு உயவே) and the Pandya's ash are his story, credited to Murugan.

914.reading: The poet describes courtesans who half-hide at the door, send small messengers to men of desire, press faces and nails, loosen their garments on the flower bed and wear young men down day after day, then swear 'this is the price, this is the truth' and turn harsh when the money given runs out, and asks whether having joined them is not enough. The praise tells of the churning of the sea with the mountain as churn and Vasuki as rope, Vishnu at one end and Vali at the other, and Lakshmi rising with the nectar, and names Murugan the bridegroom of the noble one who cuts the chain of deeds, at Vayalur.
914.nuance: விலை ஈதே கடிய சத்தியமாம் எனவே சொலி: the woman names her price and swears to it, the trade and the oath in one line. அவர் கொடப் பணம் மாறிட கடுகடுத்திடுவார், growing harsh when the money given changes, is the stock end. Vali among the churners is an unusual detail. The last lines (மறு ஒர் எட்டுடன் ஆயிரம்) are obscure.

links.note: Both set aside the quarrelling sects and ask instead for one wordless certainty, 339 for the true form filled with silence, 907 for jnana that does not waver; 907 goes further and names the Saiva paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga among the places to be lost.

The Tirumanthiram assigns chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana each to its own people, with the siddhas reaching Siva-jnana at the top. 907 keeps the order but treats the first three as traps rather than steps, asking to be given jnana without perishing in them.

Both songs are built on the refrain அலமலம், 'enough, enough'. 368 sweeps away women, patron-poetry and the sects; 908 the body itself, food, bed, wife, children and kin, keeping only kinship with those who think of the Lord.
The Kural says the good remember through seven births those who wiped away their distress; 911 makes the same vow, never to forget, toward the Lord who cut away the stain of desire and gave jnana.

Both credit Murugan with Sambandar's victory over the Jains: 913 names Sirkazhi, the Kaundinya clan and the leaf that survived the fire; 920 the leaf that swam against the current, the eight thousand impaled Jains and the Pandya king and queen.
